questions.question_text: Who may file a complaint against a Utah real estate licensee with the Division?
distractors: Only licensed real estate professionals
Only parties to the transaction
Only the Real Estate Commission
questions.explanation: 61-2f-402 lets the Division investigate on a complaint from any person, or on its own motion. The Division then decides whether to dismiss, resolve informally, or commence an adjudicative proceeding.

questions.question_text: After investigating a complaint, the Division determines a violation occurred but it was minor and unintentional. The Division may:
distractors: Only dismiss or revoke the license
Automatically revoke the license
Refer to criminal court only
questions.explanation: Investigation outcomes include dismissal, informal resolution, or a formal adjudicative proceeding under 61-2f-402. The Commission weighs seriousness, harm, cooperation, and prior history when deciding what action fits (61-2f-404(1)(b)).

questions.question_text: A buyer files a complaint alleging their agent failed to disclose a material defect. What happens first?
distractors: The agent's license is immediately suspended
The case goes directly to a hearing
The Real Estate Commission votes on guilt
questions.explanation: When a complaint is filed, the Division investigates first. A license is not suspended automatically upon receiving a complaint. Investigation results determine whether further action is warranted.

questions.question_text: During a Division investigation, a licensee refuses to provide requested records. This refusal is:
distractors: Within the licensee's legal rights
Only relevant in a criminal case
Permitted if records are older than 1 year
questions.explanation: Failing to respond to a Division request in an investigation within 10 business days — including withholding evidence or failing to produce records — is itself grounds for discipline under 61-2f-401(18). The Division may also issue subpoenas and take testimony under oath (61-2f-402(3)).

questions.question_text: A complaint investigation reveals no violation occurred. The Division will:
distractors: Issue a formal warning to the licensee
Place the licensee on probation
Report the complaint to the Commission
questions.explanation: If an investigation finds no violation, the Division will dismiss the complaint. No action is taken against the licensee, and no record of discipline is created.

questions.question_text: How often can the Division of Real Estate audit a broker's trust account?
distractors: Once per calendar year only
Only upon receiving a complaint
Every two years at renewal time
questions.explanation: 61-2f-403(1) lets the Division audit a principal broker's trust accounts at any time. If the audit shows gross mismanagement, commingling, or misuse, the Division may order a full CPA audit and the Commission may order the licensee to reimburse its cost.

questions.question_text: A principal broker has maintained trust account records but stored them at their home rather than the office. If the Division requests an audit, the broker must:
questions.correct_answer: Make the records available for inspection
distractors: Request a 30-day extension to relocate them
Provide only a summary of transactions
Refuse until a court order is obtained
questions.explanation: R162-2f-401k(2) requires records to be kept at the principal business location or a designated branch office, or electronically in a compliant storage system — not at the broker's home — and R162-2f-401k(3) requires them to be produced for the Division on request.

questions.question_text: A Division audit discovers that a broker has been mixing personal funds with client trust funds. This is called:
distractors: Conversion
Embezzlement
Misappropriation
questions.explanation: Commingling is mixing the broker's own money with client trust money. Utah draws a bright line: depositing more than $1,000 of the principal broker's own funds into a real estate trust account violates 61-2f-401(4)(b) (R162-2f-403a(13)). Conversion is using those funds for the broker's benefit.

questions.question_text: During an audit the Division finds a broker failed to deposit earnest money as Division rules require. What can follow?
questions.correct_answer: A disciplinary order imposing fines and corrective action
distractors: Nothing, if no client was harmed
Only an informal verbal warning
Termination of all active listing agreements
questions.explanation: The Commission, with the concurrence of the director, may impose a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per violation — $10,000 if the property owner was 65 or older or a vulnerable adult, or the amount of any gain — plus education, probation, suspension, or revocation (61-2f-404(1)(a)).

questions.question_text: A principal broker claims they were unaware a sales agent was not properly depositing trust funds. Is the broker still responsible?
questions.correct_answer: Yes, the PB is responsible for supervision
distractors: No, only the sales agent is liable
Only if there is a written complaint
Only if the amount exceeds $5,000
questions.explanation: 61-2f-401(13) makes failure to exercise active and reasonable supervision a violation by the principal broker, and 61-2f-406 makes an affiliated agent's violation cause for revoking, suspending, or fining the principal broker up to $5,000 per violation.

questions.question_text: Which is a ground for disciplinary action against a Utah licensee?
questions.correct_answer: Commingling trust funds with personal funds
distractors: Charging a commission below market rate
Refusing to work with a specific MLS
Declining to hold an open house
questions.explanation: Commingling trust funds is a specific ground for discipline. Commission rates are negotiable, and licensees are not required to use specific MLS systems or hold open houses.

questions.question_text: A licensee is facing formal administrative proceedings. Which law governs these proceedings?
distractors: Utah Real Estate Purchase Contract
Utah Criminal Code
Utah Uniform Commercial Code
questions.explanation: Adjudicative proceedings follow Title 63G, Chapter 4, the Utah Administrative Procedures Act (61-2f-404(3)). The Commission may hear a matter itself or delegate it to an administrative law judge or the Division (61-2f-103(2)(c)).

questions.question_text: Unless the order states otherwise, when does an order of the Division take effect?
questions.correct_answer: 30 days after the order is served
distractors: Immediately upon signature
10 days after the order is served
Only after judicial review is exhausted
questions.explanation: 61-2f-404(2)(c)(i) provides that an order, ruling, or decision becomes operative 30 days after service unless the order says otherwise. If a licensee appeals, the Division may stay enforcement under 63G-4-405.

questions.question_text: A sales agent submits a false statement on their license renewal application. This is:
questions.correct_answer: Grounds for discipline by the Division
distractors: Only a concern if discovered during audit
Permissible if the error was unintentional
Handled by the Association of REALTORS
questions.explanation: 61-2f-401(1)(a) makes a substantial misrepresentation — expressly including one in a licensure statement — grounds for discipline, and R162-2f-401b(1)(c) separately bars misrepresenting to the Division in a renewal application or an investigation.

questions.question_text: The Commission determines a licensee acted incompetently. Which sanctions may be imposed?
questions.correct_answer: Suspension, fines, education, or a combination
distractors: Only license revocation is available
Only a verbal warning may be issued
Only a fine not exceeding $500 applies
questions.explanation: 61-2f-404(1)(a) lets the Commission, with the director's concurrence, impose education, a civil penalty, revocation, suspension, probation, denial of renewal, a cease and desist order, an admonition, a reprimand, surrender with discipline pending, or any combination. Incompetence is a listed ground under 61-2f-401(7).
